b: They say we like to scare ourselves. I doubt that’s true when it comes to our finances. But there are times when Mr Market slashes at our investments anyway, like Freddy Krueger slicing and dicing a couple of hapless teenagers.
It’s time to face our fears. The best way to stop yourself panicking like an American virgin on a remote camping trip is to know just how bad things can get.
Our investigations into risk tolerance tell us how much carnage we think we can take. But how much might we have to take?
Let’s roll the tape and gawp slack-jawed at investing’s scariest horror shows.
Note: All figures are inflation-adjusted total returns in GBP unless otherwise stated.
Every asset class with a century-long record has lost more than half its real value at some point since 1900. Even cash!
I’ll prove it below by running through the drawdown-spattered charts in all their gory glory. The deeper the bloody losing streak on these charts, the more unholy the massacre.

Data from MSCI, Before the Cult of Equity 1, A Century of UK Economic Trends 2, Robert Shiller, The Big Bang 3, Bank of England, Millennium of Macroeconomic Data for the UK, 4 and ONS. October 2026. Pre-1970 World monthly returns are market-cap weighted UK and US equities returns (GBP).
Yes, even the diversified world equities index has spent almost a third of its time nursing wounds in excess of 20%.
The worst evisceration was the Great Depression (-64%) while the longest lasted 15 years and nine months from the end of 1968 through September 1984.
More recently, the bogeyman returned to torment investors with real terms losses over 50% – and 14 years in the red – from August 2000 to May 2014.
The tendency for this spine-chilling franchise to churn out sequels is why stock market survivors derisk.
Bonds: the return of the living dead
Here’s your regular reminder that bonds aren’t ‘safe’ in the way we’d normally use that word:
Data from Alan Stocker 5, British Government Securities Database, 6 FTSE Russell. Millennium of Macroeconomic Data for the UK, 7 and ONS. October 2026.

The -69% savagery in the chart associated with World War One is one thing. But the 58 years spent in negative territory (-65% low) from 1935 to 1993 is enough to make you question if the devil really is among us. (And if he’s a bond salesman.)

Notice, too, how bonds climbed out of the depths of hell as the chart ascends decisively from 1982. Anyone buying in from that point on would have seen bonds as an appreciating asset capable of giving equities a run for their money. That is until the inflation monster rose from the grave again in 2021.
Moreover, gilt owners have gotten off lightly in comparison to other country’s bondholders.
German government bonds lost everything to hyperinflation in 1922.

French bonds collapsed -98% from 1910, with that market only bottoming out 71 years later in 1981. They’re still 88% down more than a century later at the end of 2024. (See the Deutsche Bank Research Institute’s The Ultimate Guide to Long-Term Investing. Single country returns quoted in local currency.)
Japan and Italy have also visited 99% losses upon their whimpering bond investors. Once again rampant inflation shredded real returns like a knife-wielding maniac.
If bonds can turn on you, surely cash is safe?
Yep, about as safe as an isolated cabin in the woods:
Data from Millennium of Macroeconomic Data for the UK 8, A Century of UK Economic Trends 9, Bank of England, and ONS. October 2026.

Cash is the slowest killer of all. Money market funds lost -57% of their real value from May 1933 to April 1956, as inflation outran interest rates year after year. Investors didn’t make good their 1933 purchasing power until February 1991. That’s 58 years later.
Savers with high street banks and building societies fared even worse in the era before deregulation. Their real wealth fell -65% from 1933 to 1981. It is still below that 1933 peak today.

Meanwhile, the sequel is showing in a bank account near you. Cash returns trailed inflation for over 17 years from January 2009. Real drawdown reached -30% by May 2023. It was still -25% as of June 2026.
Can gold ward off the ravenous demons of market hell?
Data from Measuring Worth, GBP Gold Price 1919-68 10, The London Bullion Market Association, gold GBP spot price, Millennium of Macroeconomic Data for the UK, 11 and ONS. October 2026.
Notice how the red drains out of the gold chart circa 1970? That’s gold deregulating as it transmutes into a fully investible asset. See gold’s historical asset class returns for more.
Then what happens? Repeated gold price slashery, that’s what. With a 19-year mauling ending in a grisly -78% blood-letting (August 1999), the worst of all our GBP carve-ups.
Bizarrely a chunk of gold often helps portfolio diversification all the same. But not if you’re the nervy type.
It’s another scene from an abattoir:
Data from AQR 12, Summerhaven 13, Bloomberg, A Century of UK Economic Trends 14, Bank of England, and ONS. October 2026.
The chart is drenched with negative returns, but remember that commodities is one of the few asset classes capable of warding off inflation like a silver crucifix stymies vampires.
While too volatile on its own, commodities can offer a refuge when other assets are giving you a dark night of the soul.
Mixing equities and bonds delivers some protection but it does not vanquish all evil:
60% World equities / 40% All Stocks portfolio, rebalanced annually at the end of each December.
Here’s how a World 60/40 portfolio fared against 100% world stocks during the five worst equity slaughters since 1900:
Source: A terminally ancient investor’s blood-spattered diary found by their corpse.
Bonds cushioned the blow four out of five times. We’ll take it!
The Great Depression and Dotcom Bust in particular are two perils that look much less scary from the 60/40 investor’s perspective. Essentially, the lowest ebb is half as bad in those cases.

Meanwhile eight years is lopped off the length of the Noughties trauma. That’s rare though. Holding gilts often makes little difference to the duration of the event. Bond ownership actually increased the severity of the WW1 drawdown.

The same thing happened when stocks and bonds fell together post-Covid. Between November 2021 and October 2023, the World 60/40 lost -24% against -13% for pure world equities. That was deeper than its -19% fall in the Global Financial Crisis.
We’ve written before about the flaws in the 60/40 plan, and how you might fix them.
While few seriously question owning the world market instead of punting it all on one country nowadays, it’s worth remembering why.
The following fright nights are quoted as each country’s investors lived them: in their currency, after their inflation.

The biggest US bloodbath was the -77% inflicted during part one of the Great Depression from September 1929 to June 1932. The loss was actually 82% in nominal terms, but deflation reduced the real pain a touch.
The UK’s all-time shocker was the 1972-74 crash: a -75% gutting from April 1972 to December 1974. It wasn’t until April 1983 – 11 years after the peak – that investors got back to black.

More infamously, Japan’s bubble burst on New Year’s Eve 1989. It then subjected its equity investors to decades of torture, culminating in a -79% low. Japanese investors finally broke even in September 2021: almost 32 years after the peak. The commonly referenced Nikkei 225 price index didn’t regain its 1989 high until February 2024.
Moreover, Japanese equities have done worse before. The market lost around -99% between 1937 and 1948. Recovery took 26 years – an investing lifetime.
Spain suffered the biggest non-war shares shocker: -84% between 1974 and 1982, with 22 years to get back to square one.
Austria holds the record for the longest stock market recovery: 89 years after its -96% collapse of 1914 to 1925. The breakthrough came in 2003. The great-grandchildren must have been delighted.

France may yet beat that. French shares lost -96% between 1942 and 1950, then kept sliding for almost three more decades, for a total fall of -98%. At the end of 2025, French equities were still 15% below their 1942 peak in real terms: 83 years and counting. If they stay below it until 2031, they’ll take Austria’s record.
Germany suffered two near-wipeouts in a generation: a -92% real collapse in the two years after its 1923 hyperinflation boom, then a -90% fall in 1948 alone.
Italy’s shares lost -91% between 1906 and the 1945 low and took 53 years to recover. Then Italy did it again: -87% between 1961 and 1977.
Sweden – one of the world’s best-performing stock markets of the past century – lost -76% between 1912 and 1920 and spent 32 years in the red.
Switzerland isn’t always a safe haven. Its equities lost -69% in real terms between 1961 and 1974, and spent 31 years underwater.
While locking the doors or calling the sheriff rarely seems to hold the darkness at bay, time sometimes provides the silver bullet.
This is how often each asset lost money across every holding period starting from January 1900:
It’s always darkest before the dawn. Or maybe the dawn after that.
World stocks lost money in roughly one year in three. But no 25-year period since 1900 ended in a real loss, and over 30 years even the worst outcome more than doubled your money after inflation.

Gilts, cash, and gold, meanwhile, were losers in about four of every ten 30-year periods. Commodities sit in between: they sucked your soul about one 20-year period in six, but almost never over 30 years.
The World 60/40 portfolio is the surprise. Its bonds made it slightly less likely to lose money over five or ten years, but from 15 years on it was more likely to lose.
The difference between a scary movie and the investor gore above is that these losses are real. Literally: every figure here is after inflation.
But understanding the monsters that can stalk your portfolio is your best defence against doing the wrong thing when they show up.
Remember that none of these work:
Running away through the woods at night.
Emotional sex in a flimsy tent after your best friend was dismembered.
Selling up when the market bottoms out.
